basics.label: PhD candidate in experimental particle physics, University of Victoria
basics.name: Alexandre Beaubien
basics.summary: PhD candidate at the University of Victoria working on the Belle II experiment: a measurement of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section, a longitudinally polarized electron source for the Chiral Belle upgrade of SuperKEKB, and machine-learning tools for the electromagnetic calorimeter.

interests.name: Precision measurements of e⁺e⁻ → hadrons cross sections
polarized electron beams and the Chiral Belle upgrade of SuperKEKB
machine learning for detector simulation and particle identification

highlights: Measurement of the e⁺e⁻ → π⁺π⁻ cross section at the SuperKEKB collision energy (10.58 GeV) to extract the pion electromagnetic form factor; sole analyst, using the 365 fb⁻¹ Run 1 Υ(4S) dataset; the analysis is close to the working-group review stage. Regularly presented at Belle II working-group meetings and at General Meetings since 2024.
Built a custom BDT-based particle identification tool for pions at the full beam energy.

Measured the BDT efficiency from data for each particle type, as two-dimensional angular maps to measure the detector’s systematic effects: pions from τ → (ρ → ππ⁰)ν decays for the signal, and electrons and muons from e⁺e⁻ and μ⁺μ⁻ control samples for the backgrounds.

Studied the systematic effects of detector mis-modelling: in the KLM, removing regions with poor sensitivity from the fiducial region; in the ECL, for electron discrimination; and in the track momentum.
Redesigned the ECL and support-structure geometries in the Belle II GEANT4 simulation to resolve ECL-related volume overlaps.

Extended the MSc GAN waveform generator to all 8736 ECL crystals (one model per crystal) and wrote a prototype basf2 module (eclBGOverlaySimulator, not yet in a release) to use generated noise in simulation; presented at Belle II General Meetings (2023, 2024) and the CAP 2023 Congress.
Developed a multivariate classifier that separates BB̄ from cc̄ events using event-level kinematic and topology variables, in order to study the physics program of the Chiral Belle upgrade.
work.name: University of Victoria and the Belle II Collaboration

highlights: Designed a GaAs-based polarized electron source, from concept to final design and manufacturing, for the Touschek experiment: a polarization-lifetime measurement in the SuperKEKB High Energy Ring and the first step toward the proposed Chiral Belle upgrade. Drew its ultra-high-vacuum chamber, selected the components and assisted the KEK technicians with the assembly and bake-out.
Optimized the cathode and anode in simulation to minimize the emittance, reaching about 1.6 mm·mrad; developed the electron-beam transport simulations and designed the focusing magnets.
Designed and simulated a prototype beam merger to integrate the source into the beamline.

Supported the beam-tracking simulations: measured the dimensions and magnetic fields of the injection room, produced drawings of the room, obtained the simulation input files and coordinated between KEK and UVic.
Presented the work in an invited seminar at TRIUMF and at the CAP 2025 Congress.
work.name: KEK
work.position: Research stay: polarized electron source R&D
work.summary: KEK–TRIUMF EPECR Fellow (Exchange Program for Early Career Researchers), Jan – Mar 2025.

highlights: Developed a deep convolutional generative adversarial network (GAN) that generates noise waveforms for the ECL crystals, trained on 154,692 recorded waveforms. Generating noise for all 8736 crystals of one event takes 7.7% of the time needed to simulate and reconstruct a BB̄ event.

Developed a charged-particle identification tool based on ECL pulse-shape discrimination (PSD), with gradient-boosted decision trees trained on one million simulated particles per species: electron–pion AUC improved from 0.980 to 0.996 overall and from 0.928 to 0.978 below 1 GeV/c, outperforming basf2’s PSD classifier trained on neutral clusters. Presented at the CAP 2022 Congress; re-implemented during the PhD with 1.8 million simulated tracks, confirming the gain.

highlights: Calibrated a high-purity germanium (HPGe) detector at the SNOLAB Low Background Counting Facility, supervised by Dr. Silvia Scorza, Dr. Ian Lawson and Dr. Bruce Cleveland.
Took data with calibration sources in the SNOLAB clean laboratory and simulated the detector response in GEANT4.
Analyzed the data and simulations with ROOT in C++.

Identified the sources and rates of background in the Belle II detector by comparing the first collision data with Monte Carlo simulation.
Presented preliminary results at the McGill undergraduate poster conference (September 2018).

highlights: ECL geometry expert.

Regular ECL expert, control-room (CR) and Belle II Commissioning Group (BCG) shifts.

The project showed that autoencoder designs are cheaper and more reliable to build than GANs, but perform less well.
